1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.background: Also called the Capablanca Variation, it was popular in the early days of the Nimzo-Indian and was eventually superseded by 4.e3. It was revived in the 1990s and is now about as popular as that move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O.strategy: The most common reply: Black puts the king away and keeps every plan open. The queen on c2 has made sure White will not get doubled pawns, so Black does not hurry to give up the bishop and waits to see how White commits.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Zurich Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6.background: Also known as the Milner-Barry Variation, after the British player Stuart Milner-Barry.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn and prepares a pawn centre on d6 and e5 that leaves the other bishop free. The dark-squared bishop is given up, and the knight blocks Black's own c-pawn, which is why the move is rarer today.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre at once and attacks the c4 pawn, which the queen cannot defend because the knight on c3 is in the way. White has to decide immediately how to resolve the central tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn, which the queen on c2 no longer guards. If White defends it, Black keeps the pressure and gets an easy game, so White almost always takes, and Black then plans to win the pawn back.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.strategy: Almost forced: the d4 pawn is attacked and nothing guards it, so White takes. The pawn on c5 is exposed to the bishop, which means White will soon have to fight to keep it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.Nf.strategy: Defends d4 with a developing move, but Black keeps the pressure on the centre by taking on d4 and gets an easy game. That is why White normally takes on c5 instead.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.e3.strategy: Defends d4 with a pawn and opens the king's bishop, but it shuts in the queen's bishop and leaves Black the pressure on d4. Black gets an easy game, which is why White normally takes on c5 instead.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation, Pirc Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.background: In the mid-20th century it was one of the reasons 4.Qc2 was little played, since Black's recapture with the knight was reckoned to give easy equality. Edmar Mednis remarked that the entire Pirc Variation had become unplayable at the highest level, though players like Kramnik have been willing to defend the Black side against players like Kasparov.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.strategy: The main line: Black castles and waits to win the pawn back. Whether the bishop or a knight recaptures on c5 decides the character of the game, and White's next move decides which of the two is possible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation, Steiner Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5 5.dx.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once, to bring a knight to e4 after the recapture, where it attacks the queen and the c5 pawn together. It surrenders the bishop pair, and White keeps the extra pawn for the moment.
Regains the pawn at once with the bishop and keeps both bishops, trading the pin for a safe game with a healthy structure. White can develop freely, so Black has to find the activity later.
Wins the pawn back with a knight, which stands well on c5, while the bishop keeps its pin. It gives Black an easy game if White cannot stop it, and an early a3 forces the bishop to decide at once.

Asks the bishop to decide and takes away the manoeuvre with the knight that gave Black easy equality. The bishop will recapture on c5 or take the knight, so White keeps the bishop pair; this is the critical test of the line.
Develops, but lets Black win the pawn back with a knight: ...Na6 attacks c5 a second time while the bishop keeps its pin, and Black equalises without difficulty.
Opens the king's bishop but does nothing about the c5 pawn, which Black regains with the bishop or by bringing a knight to a6. It also shuts in the queen's bishop, so the extra pawn does not last.
Regains the pawn at once and puts the bishop on an active diagonal. Black has the pawn back and active pieces in return for the bishop pair that White keeps.

Gives up the bishop pair at once for the knight, planning to take back on c5 with a knight. The queen recaptures on the long diagonal with the pawn on c5 still White's, and White has time to defend it while keeping both bishops.
Retreats and loses a tempo: the pawn on c5 stays White's, and a pawn advance on the queenside chases the bishop again. Black is a pawn down without compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide: it must retreat or take the knight. If it takes, the queen recaptures and also guards c4, so White keeps the bishop pair with healthy pawns; this is the solid way to meet the strike in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.cx.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes the threat to c4, leaving Black the choice of recapture. White gives up the tension in the centre and the c-pawn, but the queen stays where it guards c3, and the game opens up quickly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.e3.strategy: Defends d4 and opens the king's bishop to take back on c4, a solid but passive reply. It asks the bishop no question, so Black can keep the pin or release it on its own terms, and White's play is slower.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.strategy: Takes the knight rather than retreating, giving up the bishop pair for a quick lead in development. Black wants an open game before White's bishops come to life, and the pawn structure is left whole on both sides.
Retreats and keeps both bishops, but it gives up the pin and the chance to damage White's structure. White can develop at leisure and take the centre, so Black has a solid but rather passive game.
Retreats to a more active diagonal, but the bishop can be chased with tempo by c5, which gains White space. Black keeps the bishop pair but loses time and gives White room.
The natural recapture: the queen keeps White's pawns healthy, guards c4 and keeps the two bishops. The queen is centralised but also becomes a target, so Black can look for tempo against it at once.

Recaptures with the pawn, which doubles White's c-pawns, the very weakness the queen on c2 was meant to avoid. The broad centre and the open b-file give enough play to keep the position level, but White has damaged its own structure for no real gain.
Blocks the check but loses a piece: 6...Bxd2+ takes the bishop, and the recapture only returns that bishop, so White has paid a knight and a bishop for one.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Noa Variation, Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.strategy: The main line: the knight attacks the queen, wins a tempo and takes the strong central square. Black aims for a quick opening of the position to exploit the lead in development against the two bishops, with a balanced game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Noa Variation, Botvinnik Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.strategy: Develops a piece and adds pressure on d4, but unlike the knight move to e4 it does not hit the queen. White gets time to take space with its pawns and to use its bishops, while the knight blocks Black's own c-pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Romanishin Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.a3.strategy: A gambit: Black hits d4 at once and offers a pawn. If White takes, the knight comes to e4 with tempo on both the queen and the pawn, so Black gets quick play; but it is a risky try rather than a refutation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.cx.strategy: Recaptures with the queen; the knight on c3 is pinned and cannot take it. The queen can then offer a trade of queens that strengthens Black's hold on e4 and frees e6 for the bishop, enough for equality.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.cx.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5 5.cx.strategy: Keeps a pawn in the centre and opens the e-file and the bishop on c8. The line is sharper than the queen recapture, since White's bishop can come to g5 to pin the f6 knight against the queen, so Black has to be ready for a tactical fight.

Recaptures with the knight, which the pinned knight on c3 cannot take. If the bishop takes on c3, White cannot recapture with the queen because the knight on d5 would take it, so the pawns double. In return the knight on d5 is a target for a central pawn advance, which gains White space.
Natural development, but it lets Black offer a queen trade that leaves Black comfortable. The trade gives Black equality, which makes this the weaker way to meet the queen recapture.
The way to avoid the queen trade: after ...Qf5 the bishop can go to d3 and attack the queen, so the queens stay on. The price is the bishop on c1, shut in behind the pawn on e3.

Asks the bishop to decide; if it takes, the queen recaptures and eyes the c7 pawn that Black's queen no longer covers. It spends a move on the flank while Black's queen stands in the centre, so Black gets time to organise.

Offers the exchange of queens: after the trade, the pawn recapture on f5 strengthens Black's grip on e4 and frees e6 for the bishop. The queen already attacks White's queen along the diagonal, so White must answer at once.

Adds a second attacker to d4, which only the knight on f3 guards, so White has to spend a move holding the pawn. It keeps the queens on and the tension high, with the black queen exposed in the middle.

Gives up the bishop pair to force the queen onto c3, where ...Ne4 attacks it. But the queen on c3 looks at the c7 pawn, which Black's queen no longer guards, so Black has to spend a move on it. Playable, but it hands White the bishops for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Zurich Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Protects the d4 pawn, which the knight on c6 attacks, and develops a piece. White keeps its set-up flexible and waits to see how Black builds its centre, with the unpinning of the knight still in reserve.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.e.strategy: Protects d4 with a pawn, but it shuts in the queen's bishop and leaves the king's knight at home. White is slower than with the knight move, and Black can set up its central pawns undisturbed.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.a.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide but leaves d4 unprotected: 5...Nxd4 attacks the queen, and 6.axb4? Nxc2+ costs White the queen for a bishop. After the queen retreats White is a pawn down, with its pawns doubled once ...Bxc3+ comes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Milner-Barry Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.strategy: The idea of the variation: Black prepares a pawn centre on d6 and e5, which leaves the light-squared bishop free on its diagonal. Black has accepted giving up the dark-squared bishop in return for a flexible, solid structure.
Castles first and keeps the choice of pawn structure open. It delays the central pawn plan, which can be prepared with a rook or the queen, but gives White time to unpin the knight.

Prepares the central pawn advance with the queen instead of the king: the queen stands behind the e-pawn, ready to support it, while the king stays in the middle a little longer. The d-pawn remains free to choose its square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Zurich Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Unpins the knight, so that a capture on c3 can be answered with the bishop and the queen can stay on c2. White avoids the doubled pawns it feared and is ready to close the centre if Black pushes in the middle.
Supports d4 and opens the king's bishop, the quiet way to develop. The knight on c3 stays pinned, though, and the unpinning is delayed while Black prepares the central pawn plan undisturbed.
Asks the bishop to decide. If it takes, the queen recaptures and White keeps the bishop pair, but the queen lands on c3, where ...Ne4 hits it with a tempo.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Zurich Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Solid: the pawn guards d4 and opens the king's bishop for quiet development. The knight on c3 remains pinned, but the queen on c2 means Black's bishop can only take it at the price of giving up the bishop pair.

Unpins the knight, so that a capture on c3 is answered with the bishop and the queen can stay on c2. White avoids the doubled pawns without spending time on the queen and is ready to close the centre if Black pushes in the middle.
Asks the bishop to decide. If it takes, the queen recaptures and White keeps the bishop pair, but the queen lands on c3, where ...Ne4 hits it with a tempo.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide and prepares to meet the capture with the queen. White keeps the two bishops with a healthy pawn structure, and Black has to find activity in return; this is the main line of the Classical set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.e.strategy: Quiet and solid: the pawn guards d4 and opens the king's bishop for development. White does not force the bishop's decision, so Black can keep the pin or take on c3 when it likes.

Grabs the centre at once, but the pawn on e4 depends on the queen on c2, and ...Bxc3+ leaves White the choice between doubled pawns and losing the e-pawn. The move sits ill with the queen's job and leads to sharp, theoretical play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.strategy: Settles the bishop's future at once: it trades itself for the knight instead of retreating. White gets the bishop pair and can recapture with the queen, and Black, already castled, has the lead in development to make something of it.
Retreats and keeps both bishops, but it gives up the pin and the chance to damage White's pawns. White gets the centre and the initiative, and Black's bishop is passive on e7.

Retreats to an active diagonal, but gives up the pin and the chance to double White's pawns. White's pawn can advance to e5, hitting bishop and knight together, so Black falls behind in the fight for the centre and White gets the easier game.

The recapture that 4.Qc2 was made for: White keeps the pawn structure intact and the bishop pair. The price is that the queen has now moved twice and the kingside is undeveloped, so Black will try to open the game quickly.

Recaptures with the pawn, which doubles White's c-pawns, the very weakness the queen on c2 was meant to avoid. The broad centre and the open b-file give enough play to keep the position level, but White has damaged its own structure for no real gain.
Blocks the check but loses a piece: 6...Bxd2+ takes the bishop, and the recapture only returns that bishop, so White has paid a knight and a bishop for one.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Keres Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.background: Nowadays the main line of the Classical Variation.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.strategy: Prepares the bishop for b7, where it and the f6 knight watch e4, the square White needs for a pawn centre. Black accepts that White has the two bishops and plays for control of the light squares, which leads to a manoeuvring fight over e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Vitolins-Adorjan Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.background: The gambit was invented by Alvis Vītoliņš.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a.strategy: A gambit: Black offers the b-pawn to open the queenside and gain time against the queen, since the knight can come to e4 with a hit on it once White takes. The compensation rests on activity alone, so it is a try for a lively game, not a sound way to equalise.

Strikes in the centre at once and challenges the c4 pawn. If White takes, recapturing with the knight attacks the queen on c3, so the exchange costs White time. Black has given up the bishop pair and has to make the central pawns and quick development count.

Attacks the queen and puts the knight on the central square e4 with tempo. White must spend a move on the queen, and Black can support the knight with a chain of kingside pawns. The knight is strong there, but White keeps the bishop pair as long-term compensation.
Solid but slow: it guards e5 and frees the b8 knight to come out, yet it does nothing about White's bishop pair or space. Black accepts a passive but safe position while White builds a broad centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.e.strategy: Claims a share of the centre at once and takes e4 away from White's pieces. The pawn also attacks c4, so White has to decide whether to release the tension. Black gets a solid structure and easy development in return for a little less space.

Attacks d4 before White has finished developing, so the centre has to be clarified early. The queen on c2 lets White recapture on c3 without wrecking the pawns, so Black plays for active pieces rather than for doubled pawns.

Prepares the bishop for b7, where it and the f6 knight watch e4. A flexible, quiet set-up, but it does not challenge d4 or c4, so White gets time to develop the bishop and castle and keeps the more comfortable game.

Develops the knight toward the centre, where it guards d4 and e5, and prepares to finish the kingside development. The knight on c3 is still pinned against the king by the bishop, so White wants to castle without much delay.

Settles the centre at once. After the exchange Black has a solid pawn on d5 and a half-open e-file, while White gets the half-open c-file and a clear plan of pressing on the queenside. The pin on the c3 knight stays a factor.

Asks the bishop to decide. Taking on c3 gives White the bishop pair with the queen recapturing and the pawns intact, but a rook-pawn move costs time while the kingside is undeveloped, and Black can follow by taking the c4 pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.e.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O 5.e.strategy: Hits d4 at once, the pawn that holds White's centre together, while the bishop keeps the c3 knight pinned and the white king is still in the middle. Black strikes before White is ready, and the centre will open or take shape quickly.

Releases the tension on c4: White regains the pawn with a developing move, but Black is relieved of the cramp and can strike at d4 with the c-pawn. A safe, simple way to equalise that avoids the heavier middlegame.

Brings a piece to bear on d4 and develops, but the knight blocks the c-pawn that would otherwise strike at the centre. White can finish development and settle the centre on its own terms. Sound, yet it hands White the choice of plan.
